column4: The section's wording at 87:13, “neither dies nor lives,” is repeated here for the criminal who meets his Lord; the same fire context makes the suspended state a stated outcome of judgment.
The section's phrase from 87:13 is almost fully restated: they are not brought to death and the fire's torment is not eased. This adds the explicit absence of relief to the same no-death condition.
The section's wording “neither dies nor lives” meets the image of death reaching the wrongdoer from every side while “he is not dead” (وما هو بميت); the verse makes the blocked release concrete.

The section's M-W-T dictionary note includes sleep as “death”; this verse says God takes souls at death and during sleep, then retains some and sends others back, clarifying why a recoverable sleep is unlike the fire-dweller's condition.
The section quotes this verse's claim that the afterlife is “the true life” (لهي الحيوان), grounding its contrast between the near life and lasting life in an explicit Qur'anic formulation.

The section defines life as benefit and good; here a person is first dead, then given life and light by which to walk among people, making beneficial guidance a concrete opposite of the fire-dweller's lack of life.
The section distinguishes mere non-death from real, enduring life; here those killed in God's way are explicitly said not to be dead but alive with God, a sharp contrary state.
The section asks what counts as life beyond bodily survival; here the slain are alive with their Lord and provided for, unlike the torment that has neither death nor beneficial life.

The section's B-Q-Y root note links “more enduring” with lasting life; Pharaoh uses أَبْقَىٰ for the punishment he threatens after the magicians' prostration (20:70), exposing his claim to endurance against the section's true afterlife measure.

The section's B-Q-Y root and 87:17's “more enduring” meet the magicians' answer to Pharaoh: “Allah is better and more enduring” (والله خير وأبقى). This is their explicit correction of his boast in 20:71.

The section says people prefer the near life over the lasting one; the magicians answer that they will not prefer Pharaoh over the clear proofs and say he can rule only “this worldly life” (هذه الحياة الدنيا), showing the choice under immediate threat.

The section names the purified person's lasting afterlife as the counterpart to the fire; this continuation promises Eden gardens, abiding there, as “the reward of whoever purifies himself” (جزاء من تزكى).

The section cites the fire-dwellers asking for their Lord to end their condition; the answer “you will remain” (إنكم ماكثون) makes their continued confinement explicit and echoes the section's question of what it means to remain.
The section's H-Y-Y gloss defines life as benefit and good; this verse promises “a good life” (حياة طيبة) to believing doers, giving positive content to the life denied in 87:13.
The section's H-Y-Y gloss says life means benefit and good; the command to answer God and the Messenger “to what gives you life” (لما يحييكم) presents guidance as life-giving benefit.
The section's H-Y-Y dictionary sense of life as benefit fits “in retribution there is life” (في القصاص حياة): the verse names a social good that preserves life, not just biological duration.
The section quotes the regret “if only I had sent ahead for my life” (لحياتي); in this judgment scene the speaker recognizes too late that the life worth preparing for was the enduring one.

The section calls out a false offer of permanence; Satan's “tree of eternity” and kingdom that does not decay (شجرة الخلد وملك لا يبلى) is the counterfeit lasting life against which 87:17's afterlife is measured.

The section's death-and-life roots are paired by Abraham's declaration that God “causes me to die, then gives me life” (يميتني ثم يحيين); it assigns both endpoints to God rather than to a trapped intermediate state.

The section contrasts the near world's life with what is more lasting; this verse calls wealth and children adornment of worldly life, then says the “lasting good deeds” (الباقيات الصالحات) are better with the Lord.
The section's contrast between the near life and enduring hereafter is stated directly: worldly life is only temporary enjoyment, while the next life is “the abode of permanence” (دار القرار).

The section describes choosing the near life over the lasting one; this verse names the same choice as “preferring the worldly life” (وآثر الحياة الدنيا), directly identifying the orientation behind the outcome in 87:13.

The section links preference for worldly life to the fire's no-death condition; this verse supplies the immediate consequence for the preference in 79:38, “the Fire is the abode,” completing that parallel.

The section's opposite of preferring the near life is the successful, purified person; here the one who fears standing before his Lord and restrains desire is set against the worldly-life chooser in 79:38.
The section contrasts the fire's suspended torment with the lasting good afterlife; this verse completes 79:40 by making the Garden the abode of the one who restrained desire.

The section says people prefer near life over the afterlife; this rebuke asks whether they are content with worldly life “instead of” the next, then calls its enjoyment little, making the preference and its scale explicit.

The section explains that al-dunyā is the near life preferred over the more lasting one; this verse describes people who prefer worldly life over the afterlife and turn from God's path, a direct moral counterpart.

The section's central diagnosis is preferring worldly life over the afterlife; this verse uses that precise contrast for those who have loved the worldly life over the next, tying the choice to disbelief.

The section's D-N-W note says the world is named for nearness and its B-Q-Y note for lasting; this verse calls worldly provision a flower and says what is with the Lord is “better and more enduring” (خير وأبقى).

The section's secondary H-Y-W dictionary sense describes water that revives what it touches; this verse asks the reader to see God revive earth after its death and says He is the reviver of the dead, a close Qur'anic image of life after non-life.

The section places preference for worldly life beside remembering the Lord in 87:15; this verse describes one who turns away from the reminder and wants only “the life of this world” (الحياة الدنيا), joining the same two sides of the section's choice.

The section describes people choosing the near life over the afterlife; this verse identifies those satisfied with worldly life and heedless of God's signs, the stance that leads into the fire named in 10:8.
The section connects preference for worldly life with the fire's dead-end condition; this verse gives the consequence for the heedless in 10:7, making Hell their abode for what they earned.

The section contrasts the near life with the lasting afterlife; this verse distinguishes the person who wants the immediate world and is given some of it from the one who seeks the next life in 17:19.

The section presents the afterlife as the lasting alternative to near-world preference; this verse names the believer who seeks the next life and strives for it, supplying the other side of the choice introduced in 17:18.

The section sets real endurance against a false promise of immortality; this verse says no human before Muhammad was granted eternal life, bounding the promise of Satan's “tree of eternity” in 20:120.

The section's life-and-endurance contrast is sharpened by the command to rely on “the Living who does not die” (الحي الذي لا يموت); God's unending life is unlike the condemned person's state of neither living nor dying.

The section's “does not die” wording can name either torment or true blessed life; here Garden-dwellers do not taste death there after the first death and are protected from Hell, separating joyful permanence from suspended punishment.
The section's B-Q-Y note concerns what remains; this verse says all on earth pass away, setting up the boundary completed in 55:27 between transient life and what truly remains.
The section's B-Q-Y root for remaining is explicit in the Lord's face “remaining” (ويبقى وجه ربك); it gives a source of permanence beyond the transient life set out in 55:26.

The section's secondary H-Y-W gloss joins water with the revival of whatever it touches; this verse says every living thing was made from water, giving a distinct Qur'anic water-and-life relation without claiming the same Paradise setting.

The section's M-W-T dictionary entry describes being struck down and then recovering; Moses falls unconscious (خر موسى صعقا) and then wakes (أفاق), a precise Qur'anic scene parallel to that recoverable state.
The section's H-Y-Y gloss calls life a benefit; this verse says saving one person is like saving all humankind, making the value of preserving life explicit.
The section contrasts near-world enjoyment with what lasts; this verse says whatever was given is only worldly enjoyment and “what is with God is better and more lasting” (خير وأبقى).
The section's B-Q-Y gloss and 87:17 point to what endures; this verse calls what is with God better and more lasting than worldly enjoyment for those who believe and rely on their Lord.
The section describes the afterlife as better and more lasting; this verse calls lasting righteous deeds (والباقيات الصالحات) better as reward and return with the Lord.
The section's B-Q-Y root names what remains; this verse says Abraham's declaration was made a “lasting word” (كلمة باقية) among his descendants, showing a different, transmitted form of endurance.

The section introduces the magicians' prostration and confession before Pharaoh's threat in 20:71; this verse is the act of prostration itself, linking the section's prayer-and-purification choice to the later refusal to trade faith for near life.

The section contrasts the fire-bound with the purified person's lasting outcome; this neighboring promise says a believer who comes with good deeds receives the high degrees, giving the positive side before 20:76 names the gardens.

After the no-death and unrelieved torment in 35:36, the people ask to be brought out to do right, while the answer recalls that they were given a lifetime; this makes their lost chance at beneficial life concrete.

The section says the fire's victim cannot die and so cannot leave the torment; here burned skin is replaced so the punishment can continue. That is a specific bodily mechanism for sustained torment, though the verse does not use the no-death formula.
The section's fire-dwellers have no release through death; here every attempt to leave Hell from anguish is met by return to it, a separate but concrete form of being unable to escape the condition.
The section's M-W-T dictionary includes sleep as death-like; this verse says God takes people at night and raises them by day, a recurring Qur'anic formulation of sleep followed by return.

The section notes that the M-W-T root can name sleep and says the fire-dweller has no sleep; this verse says sleep was made “rest” (سباتا), identifying the restorative pause absent from that condition.

The section's sleep gloss and its exclusion of sleep in the fire meet this verse's pairing of sleep as repose with daytime rising (والنوم سباتا وجعل النهار نشورا), a normal cycle withheld from the condemned.
The section distinguishes death from a recoverable interval; this man is made dead for a hundred years and then raised, a full death-and-return boundary against the fire's refusal of either endpoint.
The section's H-Y-W dictionary branch describes water reviving what it touches; this verse says rain revives the earth after its death, a natural scene that makes the water/life link visible.
The section names a dictionary sense in which water gives life; here water from the sky revives earth after its death, another direct Qur'anic formulation of that relation.

The section's Paradise-water gloss turns on water restoring life; this verse has the questioners acknowledge that God sends rain and revives the earth after its death, a repeated but distinct earthly instance.

The section's H-Y-W dictionary branch links water and revival; this verse places rain that revives earth after its death among God's signs, giving the same life-after-death relation in a different scene.
The section names water that revives what it touches; this verse includes rain reviving earth after its death among signs for people who reason, another direct formulation of that link.

The section's water-and-life dictionary sense is echoed when rain makes barren earth stir, swell, and grow every kind; the verse itself uses that scene to establish resurrection, joining provision to life after lifelessness.

The section calls this world's life near and contrasts it with what lasts; this verse pictures worldly life as rain-grown plants that dry and scatter, a concrete image of transience that also recalls 87:4–5.
The section contrasts the near life with what lasts; this verse calls worldly life only play and amusement and says the next life's home is better for the God-fearing, giving the same valuation.

The section's selection is between near life and afterlife; this verse calls worldly enjoyment little and says the afterlife is better for the one who is mindful, specifying the measure behind that choice.

The section describes people preferring the near life; this verse lists its adornments and says they are only worldly-life enjoyment while the good return is with God, exposing the short reach of those desires.

The section contrasts worldly life with the lasting next life; this verse says people rejoice in worldly life while its enjoyment is little compared with the afterlife, making the difference in duration explicit.

The section says the near life can be preferred to the lasting one; this verse distinguishes the person who seeks the harvest of the afterlife from one who seeks the harvest of this world and receives only some of it.

The section divides worldly life from the enduring afterlife; this verse depicts worldly life as growth that yellows and becomes debris, and its pasture-like decay also recalls 87:4–5, giving the near life a concrete passing form.

The section's B-Q-Y root describes being left alive rather than wiped out; this verse values the lawful remainder of a transaction over cheating, showing how “what remains” can be a remnant of provision, not a lifespan.

The section's B-Q-Y note equates a long remaining time with living; this verse says some wish for a thousand years of life, yet such length would not remove them from punishment, distinguishing duration from true enduring life.
The section says the hereafter is the lasting life; these speakers deny it and claim there is only worldly life, “we die and live” (نموت ونحيا), a direct contrary account of the endpoints.

The section treats the afterlife as real and enduring; these speakers claim there is only worldly life and that time destroys them, a direct denial of the resurrection that gives the section's choice its stakes.

The section's H-Y-Y dictionary note glosses “they keep your women alive” as sparing them; Moses recalls Pharaoh's killing the sons while keeping the women alive, the exact survival sense the section names.

The section's H-Y-Y gloss explains Pharaoh's “keeping your women alive” as sparing them; this verse recounts the same selective killing and preservation, giving the dictionary sense its Qur'anic scene.
The section's H-Y-Y dictionary gloss says Pharaoh's “keeping women alive” means preserving them; Moses recalls that same policy here, where sons were killed and women spared.
The section names the H-Y-Y sense “keep alive”; this verse says Pharaoh killed the sons of one group while sparing its women, a precise example of life preserved under oppression.

The section's H-Y-Y note uses Pharaoh's sparing of women to explain “keep alive”; here Pharaoh orders the believers' sons killed and women spared, repeating the specific survival sense in another part of the Moses story.

The section's H-Y-Y gloss calls life benefit and good, while its B-Q-Y gloss turns on what remains; this verse says flood scum disappears but what benefits people remains on earth, joining those two roots in a precise image of enduring benefit.

The section's life-and-death roots are paired in this confession by people already confronting judgment: they say God caused them to die twice and live twice, then admit their sins and ask for a way out. It gives a real sequence of endpoints against 87:13's suspended state.

The section says choosing the near life leaves the lasting afterlife; this verse describes people who want worldly life and its adornment and receive their deeds' full measure in this life, with 11:16 stating what they lack afterward.
This continuation of 11:15 says such people have nothing in the afterlife except Fire and that their works come to nothing, a direct consequence for the worldly-life choice developed in the section.
The section calls the present life al-dunyā and says people prefer it to what lasts; this verse rebukes loving the immediate life, beginning the same contrast completed in 75:21.
This verse completes 75:20 by saying the immediate life is loved while the afterlife is left behind, a concise parallel to the section's near-life preference.

The section says people prefer the near life over the lasting afterlife; this verse similarly says people love the immediate life and leave behind a heavy day, making the deferred consequence explicit.
The section sets the fire-bound against the one who is purified; this verse says the most God-fearing will be kept far from the Fire, the direct reverse of the section's punishment scene.
The section names purification as the outcome opposed to the fire; this verse describes the God-fearing person as giving wealth to purify himself, specifying the act behind that outcome.

This verse says the giver does not act to repay anyone's favor; within the purification passage adjacent to 92:18, it clarifies that the deed is directed beyond worldly exchange, fitting the section's turn from near-life gain.
The section's 87:15 pairs remembering the Lord with prayer; this verse says the giver seeks only the face of the Most High, specifying the orientation of the purified deed in 92:18.
This verse concludes the same purification passage by promising that the God-fearing giver will be satisfied, the contented outcome opposite the Fire's no-life condition.

The section recalls Pharaoh boasting that his punishment would be more enduring; this verse says Pharaoh's people are exposed to the Fire morning and evening before the Hour's severe punishment, showing the lasting fate behind that boast.

The section contrasts near worldly life with what lasts, and 87:4–5 shows pasture turning to dark debris; this verse explicitly likens worldly life to rain-grown vegetation that dries and is carried away, repeating that passing scene.

The section's M-W-T gloss defines death as strength departing and its H-Y-Y gloss ties life to benefit; this verse says some are returned to feeblest old age and lose knowledge after having it, depicting diminished capacity before death.

The section's M-W-T root gloss centers on strength leaving; this verse traces humans from weakness to strength and back to weakness and gray hair, showing a loss of force within life rather than the fire's blocked death.

The section diagnoses preferring the near life over the afterlife; this verse says some have bought worldly life in exchange for the next and that their punishment will not be lightened, an exact choice-and-consequence parallel.

The section contrasts worldly life with the afterlife; this verse says one who seeks the reward of this world receives some of it, while one who seeks the reward of the afterlife receives it, making the chosen horizon explicit.

The section says the afterlife is better and more enduring than worldly life; this verse asks who seeks worldly reward and answers that with God is the reward of both this world and the next, placing worldly gain against the fuller source of reward.

The section explains that people choose the near life; this verse says they know only the outward aspect of worldly life while heedless of the afterlife, describing the narrowed perception behind that preference.

The section rebukes preferring worldly life over the enduring afterlife; this verse commands seeking the Hereafter through what God has given while not forgetting one's share of this world, adding a boundary that the choice concerns priority rather than erasing worldly life.

The section's M-W-T and H-Y-Y roots name death and life as distinct endpoints; this verse recounts being dead, then given life, then dying and being raised again, a concrete sequence unlike the condemned state that reaches neither endpoint.
The section centers on a person unable to pass into death or life; this verse describes a people made to die and then restored to life, a direct contrary passage through the two endpoints.

The section quotes the post-judgment regret for not having sent ahead for one's life; here, when death comes, the speaker asks to be sent back so he can do right, the same regret framed as an impossible return.
This verse answers the return request in 23:99 with a barrier until resurrection, giving a specific boundary between death and renewed earthly life that sharpens the section's missed-life regret.

The section's secondary H-Y-W dictionary sense describes water in Paradise reviving what it touches; this verse says rain is sent to revive a dead land and provide drink for people and animals, a direct water-gives-life scene with provision as its benefit.

After the rain and garden scene in 50:9–10, this verse calls the revived dead town provision for servants and says resurrection will likewise occur, connecting water-given life with the section's life-after-death image.

The section's secondary water gloss describes revival by water; this verse has wind carry clouds, rain revive a dead town, and compares that revival to resurrection, making the life-after-death relation explicit.

The section names a H-Y-W branch associating water with life; this verse says God created every moving creature from water, a specific creation-side counterpart to the dictionary's water-that-revives sense.

The section's central phrase suspends a person between death and life; this verse calls the things invoked besides God dead, not living, providing the clear dead pole for comparison while its own context concerns powerless idols.

The section's H-Y-Y gloss gives life the sense of benefit and good; this verse says the living and dead are not equal, alongside the contrast of the blind and seeing, using life and death for opposed responsiveness rather than the fire's intermediate state.
